title: How well does a small maritime segmentation network find floating obstacles, and what do fog and sun glint cost? MaSTr1325 on a CPU
lede: an LR-ASPP MobileNetV3 trained on MaSTr1325 scores 0.97 mIoU on held-out sequences yet finds only 32% of 204 floating obstacles (60% of those over 16 px); uniform fog at transmission 0.15 cuts large-object recall to 23%, fog-and-glint augmentation holds it at 61% (same fog model), and glint triples false alarms on open water for the clean-trained net
summary: Milestone 9a of track 23 (marine-detect), filed under the marine-hull programme. Public MaSTr1325 data (Bovcon et al. 2019, CC BY 4.0), split by blocks of 25 consecutive frames to avoid near-duplicate leakage (1025 train, 300 test), at 320×240 on 4 CPU cores. Models: LR-ASPP on an ImageNet MobileNetV3-Large backbone, trained clean and with fog plus glint augmentation, and a per-pixel colour-and-row MLP; 3 seeds each. Beyond pixel IoU, a MODS-style detection score from the masks: a floating obstacle (an obstacle component ringed by water, not touching the frame) is found when half its pixels are predicted obstacle; a false alarm is a predicted blob of 4+ px wholly on water. Fog is the Koschmieder scattering model with uniform transmission; glint is stylised saturating highlights with swept strength (no sourced glint statistics). Result: mIoU 0.967 but 32% of 204 floating obstacles found (173 are under 16 px, found 27%; 31 larger ones, 60%); fog at t = 0.15 cuts large-object recall to 23% while mIoU stays 0.88; augmentation keeps it at 61–65% on the same fog model; glint raises the clean net's false alarms from 0.08 to 0.28 per frame and leaves recall flat. Preliminary: reduced resolution, no IMU channel, not a reproduction of WaSR or the MODS protocol, one harbour in fair weather, uniform fog. Research code, not a certified perception system.
